title: Vidya Malavade Opens Up About Oestrogen Belly at 53: What Women Should Know
excerpt: The Chak De India actress speaks candidly about hormonal weight changes during menopause, joining a growing number of Indian public figures breaking the silence on women's health.
body:
• Bollywood actress Vidya Malavade, 53, has spoken openly about experiencing "oestrogen belly" — the hormonal weight gain around the midsection that commonly affects women during perimenopause and menopause.
  • Declining oestrogen levels during menopause shift fat storage from hips and thighs to the abdomen, increasing visceral fat and raising risks of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.
  • Malavade, known for her role in Chak De India, has consistently advocated for body acceptance and has shared her own strategies including yoga, breathing exercises, and managing cortisol through lifestyle changes.
  • Experts recommend a combination of strength training, cardiovascular exercise, protein-rich diets, and stress management to address menopausal weight changes.

Vidya Malavade has never been one to hide behind the filtered perfection of celebrity social media. The Chak De India actress, now 53, has added her voice to a growing conversation about a health topic that affects millions of women but rarely gets discussed in Indian public life: oestrogen belly, the hormonal redistribution of body fat that accompanies menopause.

In a recent disclosure, Malavade opened up about the changes in her own body, describing the abdominal weight gain she has experienced. She has previously spoken on Instagram about accepting her changing body, writing candidly: "The layer of fat around my belly — it's the biggest I have ever been. Taken me a while to be okay with my changing body."

What Is Oestrogen Belly?

The term describes the shift in fat distribution that occurs as oestrogen levels decline during perimenopause and menopause, typically between ages 45 and 55. Where younger women tend to store fat around the hips and thighs, falling oestrogen redirects fat storage to the abdomen. This isn't just a cosmetic change — the resulting increase in visceral fat, which surrounds internal organs, raises the risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers.

"During this stage, visceral fat and fat around the abdomen and thighs tend to increase, making it difficult for women to lose weight," explains Dr. Irfana Shahul Hameed, obstetrician and gynaecologist. "This happens due to the shift in estrogen levels, which can lead to fatigue, extreme cravings, and additional weight gain."

The Cortisol Connection

Malavade has previously highlighted another factor that compounds the problem: cortisol, the stress hormone. In an Instagram post, she explained the link plainly. "Cortisol will not let you lose weight, especially belly fat," she said. "When you're anxious, cortisol rises. When we stare at our phones incessantly, cortisol rises. Even the ting-ting of messages will make it rise."

"You may be exercising and eating well, but if the nervous system never gets to relax, fat loss slows down."

— Dr. Richa Bharadwaj, Consultant, Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Wockhardt Hospitals

Dr. Bharadwaj confirms that chronic stress can disrupt menstrual cycles, trigger emotional eating, encourage visceral fat accumulation, and make weight changes during mid-life hormonal shifts particularly frustrating. The combination of declining oestrogen and elevated cortisol creates a double burden for women navigating menopause.

What Helps

Exercise remains one of the most effective interventions, though the approach matters. Dr. Stephanie McNally of Northwell's Katz Institute for Women's Health recommends a three-pronged approach: cardiovascular exercise for heart health, weight training to maintain bone density and muscle mass, and balance work to prevent falls — a risk that increases with age.

"As our metabolism slows, the weight's not going to shift off the scale," McNally says. "It's about reframing that for other health benefits. Is your body composition changing? Is your strength changing? Does your cardiovascular health improve?"

Malavade's own approach combines yoga — which she practices regularly and credits for both physical and mental resilience — with practical stress management. She keeps her phone permanently on silent, practices Bhramari pranayama (humming bee breath) before sleep, and hums throughout the day when she feels her cortisol rising. "It doesn't even have to make sense. Energizing yet calming," she says.

Breaking the Silence in India

Malavade joins a growing number of Indian public figures addressing menopause openly. Shark Tank India's Namita Thapar has spoken about perimenopause complications, while actress Tisca Chopra has challenged the societal tendency to define women by their reproductive function. "So what if I ran out of eggs? There is so much more to me," Chopra has said.

For the millions of Indian women navigating menopause — often without adequate medical guidance or cultural permission to discuss it — these conversations carry practical weight. Dr. Hameed emphasizes that the weight gain is not irreversible. "With the right guidance, including proper nutrition and targeted exercise, weight loss, especially around the abdomen and thighs, can be effectively managed," she says.

Malavade's message is simpler. No filters, no pretences, no judgment — of herself or anyone else. "It's about being inclusive and allowing each one to choose the way one wants to be and accepting them the way they are," she has written. At 53, she is proving that visibility on this topic matters as much as any medical intervention.
